source.title_on_document: Is ChatGPT detrimental to innovation? A field experiment among university students

supplement.where: Supporting documents with the consent-form screenshot and experimental script (PDF p. 9, Methods, lines 196-198); S1 experimental script (PDF p. 11, lines 238-239); appendix II (PDF p. 14, Results, lines 300-301). No direct supplement URL is printed.
supplement.holds: The experimental script and consent material, and additional innovation tests described as statistically insignificant. These materials are absent from the saved PDF, so additional outcomes, statistics, instructions and any additional standard errors cannot be checked. The saved PDF does contain Figures 1-6 and Tables 1-4 as appended image pages (PDF pp. 23-32); Table 2 contains the innovation regressions (PDF p. 30).

paper_design_summary: Senior undergraduates in two existing courses at an Egyptian public university wrote graded essays with ChatGPT or without it; the authors call course enrollment the unit of randomization (PDF pp. 7-8, Methods). One week after the essays, the same study continued with a laboratory lemonade-stand game in which participants chose sales strategies and wrote advertising messages; strategy variation was computed and message creativity was rated by external annotators (PDF pp. 9-10). This is an intended test of effects after prior AI use, although the saved document does not explicitly establish that AI was unavailable during the laboratory task (PDF p. 5, Theory; PDF pp. 9-10, Methods).

studies.label: Course-level ChatGPT essay intervention with delayed laboratory innovation outcomes

assignment.what_was_assigned: The authors explicitly call enrollment in the two existing courses the unit of randomization: Social Network Analysis received ChatGPT and Data Mining was the control. The allocation is between courses, not within students. The field_rct/yes codes record the authors' randomization claim; the procedure used to allocate the courses by chance is not stated (PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 169-181; PDF p. 17, Discussion, lines 371-377).
assignment.quote: We used the enrollment in either of these two courses as our unit of randomization to assign participants to either the treatment or the control.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 169-181; PDF p. 17, Discussion, lines 371-377.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 7, Methods, lines 154-155, explicitly calls the experiment pre-registered; also PDF p. 16, Discussion, lines 360-363. No registration identifier, link or registered outcome hierarchy is given.

arms.name: ChatGPT essays (Social Network Analysis course)
arms.description: Students enrolled in Social Network Analysis were asked to write the essay assignments using ChatGPT (PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 176-181); researchers created accounts for them (PDF p. 9, lines 182-189). Table 1 describes 50 analyzed people in this arm after the payout-information exclusion and before the additional outlier exclusions (PDF p. 29); its final analyzed arm count is not reported.

arms.name: No-ChatGPT essays (Data Mining course)
arms.description: Students enrolled in Data Mining completed the essay assignments with ChatGPT neither mentioned nor allowed (PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 176-181). Table 1 describes 43 analyzed people in this arm after the payout-information exclusion and before the additional outlier exclusions (PDF p. 29); its final analyzed arm count is not reported.

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 94 initially recruited subjects, not a count explicitly at random assignment. One was discarded for missing information during payouts (PDF p. 11, Results, lines 242-244). Table 1 describes 93 analyzed people after that exclusion: control 43 and ChatGPT 50 (PDF p. 29, Observations row). Two anomalous observations were subsequently removed using the 1.5xIQR rule (PDF p. 12, lines 254-256). Table 2 reports 91 observations in each innovation regression, representing 91 analyzed people because the outcome is subject-specific (PDF p. 13, lines 272-276; PDF p. 30). Final arm counts, the excluded subjects' arms, and people analyzed specifically in the slogan and component nonparametric tests are not reported; those counts remain null.
participants.who: Senior undergraduates at an Egyptian public university, with a social-sciences major and social science computing minor, enrolled in Social Network Analysis or Data Mining (PDF pp. 7-8, Methods, lines 154-155 and 169-171).
participants.quote: A total of 94 subjects were initially recruited for the experiment. However, one subject was discarded due to missing information during payouts.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 7-8, Methods; PDF p. 11, Results, lines 242-244; PDF p. 12, lines 254-256; PDF p. 29, Table 1; PDF p. 30, Table 2, Observations row.

ai_tool.how_used: Treatment students were asked to use ChatGPT to write their graded essays, and the researchers created accounts using foreign cell phone numbers (PDF pp. 8-9, Methods, lines 176-189). Coded as open_chat because participants used ChatGPT themselves; no supplied idea bank, coaching-only protocol or inline suggestion interface is described. The model, prompts and detailed usage restrictions are not stated. The scored outcomes came from a later laboratory task; AI access during that task is not explicitly documented.

task.description: The intervention consisted of three graded essay assignments. The scored follow-up was a lemonade-stand innovation game combining constrained sales-strategy exploration with creative writing: choose stand location, lemonade color, sugar content, lemon concentration and price, and write an advertising message or slogan of at most 20 words. Sugar, lemon concentration and price were each chosen on a scale from 0 to 10. Participants could retain or change strategies after profit feedback. Slogans were rated after the sessions and did not affect payoffs (PDF p. 10, Methods, lines 204-223). No creativity or diversity scores for the intervention essays are reported.
task.duration: Three graded essays over one month during term time in April 2023 (PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 176-181); laboratory follow-up one week after all assignments were submitted (PDF p. 9, lines 190-191); seven game rounds (PDF p. 10, lines 204-206). No session duration in minutes is stated.

outcomes.name: Creativity of lemonade-stand advertising messages
outcomes.measure_detail: Four external annotators, unaware of the research question and experimental design, rated the advertising messages (PDF p. 10, Methods, lines 218-223). Methods gives a 0 to 10 creativity scale, whereas Results gives a 1 to 10 innovation scale (PDF p. 14, lines 295-298); this discrepancy remains unresolved. Results reports 265 unique messages because participants sometimes retained their message between rounds. This is the descriptive message corpus, not a confirmed number of observations in the statistical analysis. The paper does not say whether its Mann-Whitney test uses message scores, individual ratings or scores aggregated by participant, or how the four coders' ratings were combined; both unit and n_units are therefore null. Figure 3 has plotted arm levels and error bars without numeric estimate labels or a definition of the bars (PDF p. 25).
outcomes.delay: One week after all essay assignments were submitted (PDF p. 9, Methods, lines 190-191). The later session is confirmed, but the saved document does not state whether AI access was removed or prohibited while the laboratory outputs were produced (PDF pp. 9-11, Methods). question and ai_available_when_produced remain null pending the S1 experimental script or explicit laboratory instructions; the stated spillover intention (PDF p. 5, Theory, lines 92-95) does not establish an unassisted task.

contrasts.reported: Mann Whitney U test, p-value > 0.05; no significant difference in advertising-message creativity. Results reports 265 unique messages and four coders. Figure 3 has plotted arm levels and error bars, with no printed numerical arm means, SDs, intervals or definition of the bars. The U statistic and exact p-value are not printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 14, Results, lines 295-302; PDF p. 25, Figure 3; rating procedure: PDF p. 10, Methods, lines 218-223.

outcomes.name: Aggregate exploration of lemonade-stand sales strategies
outcomes.measure_detail: Computed within-person strategy variation, described as the average, subject-specific standard deviation of choices for sugar content, lemon concentration and price (PDF p. 13, Results, lines 272-276). Coded as flexibility because it represents variety within a participant's strategies; it is a dispersion proxy, not a count of conceptual categories or diversity across people. automated_score denotes this fixed arithmetic innovation score, not a language-model judge. Table 2 provides unadjusted and covariate-adjusted variants of the same outcome, each analyzing 91 people; n_units is null because the observation is a person and that count is in participants.n_analyzed (PDF p. 30). The table says results are clustered by Subject ID, rather than by the assigned course. Figure 2 plots arm levels and undefined error bars without numeric estimate labels (PDF p. 24). The text calls the difference approximately 0.6 to 0.72 standard deviation points (PDF p. 13), but no between-participant standardizer is documented. The scale and exact aggregation need clarification before standardized-effect extraction; no standardized effect was calculated or assumed. The parenthesized Table 2 quantities are not explicitly labeled as standard errors, so regression_coefficient_se is not coded; the printed coefficients and parenthesized quantities are retained in reported.

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three study-level screening criteria in the saved preprint. The authors explicitly call course enrollment the unit of randomization to ChatGPT-assisted versus no-ChatGPT essay writing (PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 169-181; PDF p. 17, Discussion, lines 371-377). This is an author-reported course-level randomized design; the chance-allocation mechanism remains unreported and is an eligibility-relevant follow-up for criterion 1. Table 2 reports 91 analyzed people in each main innovation regression, exceeding the 50-person threshold; the outcome is subject-specific (PDF p. 13, Results, lines 272-282; PDF p. 30, Table 2). Creativity was scored on participants' own advertising messages by external annotators (PDF p. 10, Methods, lines 218-223; PDF p. 14, Results, lines 295-300), satisfying criterion 3 independently of the unresolved slogan-analysis unit. The slogan test's people count is not separately reported, and 265 denotes messages, not people or confirmed test observations. All outcome questions and laboratory AI-availability fields are null: later timing alone does not establish that AI was removed (PDF p. 9, lines 187-198; PDF pp. 10-11). This affects with_ai versus after_ai coding, not the three study-level eligibility criteria. Table 2's parenthesized quantities are unlabeled and its stated Subject ID clustering differs from course-level assignment; core inclusion does not establish usable precision for pooling. The later journal version has not been screened.

one_line_finding: Strategy exploration was lower after ChatGPT-assisted coursework (91 analyzed people; coefficients -0.719 (0.326) and -0.604 (0.328), with parentheses unlabeled; PDF p. 30, Table 2), while slogan creativity showed no significant difference (Mann Whitney U p-value > 0.05; PDF p. 14).
open_questions: Slogan analysis unit: were scores analyzed per message, per rating, or after aggregation by participant, how were the ratings combined, and which people were included? The 265-message corpus does not establish the test unit or test sample (PDF pp. 10 and 14; PDF p. 25, Figure 3).

Laboratory AI availability: confirm whether AI access was prevented or removed during production of the follow-up strategies and slogans, and whether account access continued between the intervention and follow-up. The saved text describes an intended spillover test but does not print these restrictions; obtain S1 (PDF pp. 5 and 9-11).
Verify how the two courses were allocated by chance. The source calls course enrollment the unit or criterion of randomization but gives no allocation mechanism or sequence (PDF pp. 8 and 17).

Obtain the post-exclusion arm counts and the separate people counts for the slogan and component tests. Table 1 gives the earlier 43 control/50 ChatGPT split, whereas Table 2 gives only the final total of 91 (PDF pp. 11-12 and 29-30).

Obtain S1, appendix II and the preregistration. The saved PDF lacks the cited script, additional nonsignificant innovation tests and a registration identifier or primary-outcome hierarchy (PDF pp. 7, 9, 11, 14 and 16).
Resolve the 0 to 10 versus 1 to 10 slogan rating scale and define the figure error bars (PDF pp. 10 and 14; PDF pp. 23-25, Figures 1-3).

Confirm the aggregation and raw scale of strategy exploration, whether any between-participant standardization was performed, and what the parenthesized regression quantities represent. Clustering by Subject ID does not reflect course-level assignment (PDF p. 13; PDF pp. 23-24; PDF p. 30, Table 2).
Compare the saved April 5, 2024 bioRxiv preprint with the later journal version identified by the search record. No verified journal-version differences are available from the supplied files.
notes: Finalized 2026-10-09 against the saved April 5, 2024 bioRxiv preprint, not the later journal version. Read all 885 markdown lines, including references and trailing figure/table placeholders. Checked the source passages with PyMuPDF text extraction and inspected all appended figures and tables as images in memory. The PDF has 32 physical pages: main text and references on pp. 1-22, Figures 1-6 on pp. 23-28, and Tables 1-4 on pp. 29-32; it has no embedded files. find_tables returned no tables for the image-only table pages. All retained participant counts and reported outcome statistics were checked against the PDF. The assignment and people challenges contain no problems; all three outcome-challenge problems were corrected. Final counts count challenge problems, not changed fields or the separate unresolved research questions in final.open_items. All five outcome question and AI-availability fields are null pending explicit laboratory access instructions; delayed timing alone does not establish after_ai. The 265 unique messages are retained as a descriptive corpus only; slogan unit and n_units are null. For participant-level strategy outcomes n_units is null, and the confirmed 91 analyzed people in the aggregate regressions are recorded at study level and in reported statistics. Table 2 coefficients and parenthesized quantities are transcribed without an unverified standard-error tag or standardized-effect claim. Course-level randomization remains author-reported, with its mechanism an eligibility-relevant open item. Subject ID clustering does not match course-level assignment. The five named creativity/innovation outcomes are retained; the separate strategy components are separately tested outcomes, while unadjusted and adjusted aggregate regressions are variants of one outcome. No across-person diversity measure or creativity score for the intervention essays is reported. Risk behavior and voluntary strategy-recording effort do not score creativity/diversity on creative output and are omitted. The cited S1 and appendix II are absent, and additional innovation tests cannot be inventoried. No primary-outcome hierarchy is stated in the saved document. Every original open question and the unresolved slogan-unit difference are assessed in final.open_items, including the failed agreed-field confirmation of laboratory AI availability. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as historical audit evidence; its earlier statements retaining after_ai are superseded by the final coding and challenge resolutions. No effect sizes, missing counts or graph estimates were calculated. Only forms/c790.json was written.

This affects question coding, not the three study-level screening criteria.

Course allocation by chance (open_questions[2]; PDF pp. 8 and 17). Author confirmation of the allocation mechanism or the original allocation record would settle whether the courses were assigned randomly. This bears directly on criterion 1: the current met decision follows the authors' explicit randomization claim, and confirmed nonrandom assignment would change it.

Post-exclusion arm counts, excluded subjects' arms and separate people counts for slogan and component tests (open_questions[3]; PDF pp. 11-12 and 29-30). Aggregate strategy-exploration computation, raw scale and any between-participant standardization (part of open_questions[6]; PDF p. 13 and Figures 1-2). Posted data and analysis code would settle the aggregation and standardizer. This affects effect-size extraction; the participant count and existence of an output-based innovation measure are already established.

Identity of the parenthesized regression quantities and precision appropriate to course-level assignment (part of open_questions[6]; PDF p. 30, Table 2). Authors could label the quantities and supply or explain inference reflecting the allocation unit. This affects pooling suitability, not the three screening criteria.
